answers.question: For a fictional new sanitary drain in NYC, a two-inch horizontal pipe runs 20 feet and drops two inches uniformly. Is that enough fall?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:28

No. For horizontal drainage piping, the minimum slope for a 2-inch pipe is 1/4 inch per foot (PC § 704.1). Over 20 feet, that requires 5 inches of fall; the proposed 2 inches is only 1/10 inch per foot, so it falls short by 3 inches.

answers.question: Correction: it is a four-inch pipe, and it drops three inches over that same 20-foot run. Does that satisfy the minimum slope?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:34

Yes: a 4-inch horizontal drainage pipe requires at least 1/8 inch per foot, and the proposed 3-inch fall over 20 feet is 3/20 = 0.15 inch per foot—more than the 0.125-inch-per-foot minimum (PC § 704.1).

answers.question: On that same drain, can we reduce from four inches to three inches farther downstream because there is less room? This is the main horizontal line, not a toilet outlet connection.
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:30

Possibly, but the supplied rules don’t establish that it’s acceptable without the load and slope for the 3-inch downstream portion. For a building drain or sewer, Table 710.1(1) limits the drainage fixture units connected to each portion by pipe diameter and slope: a 3-inch pipe carries up to 36 DFU at 1/8 inch per foot, 42 at 1/4 inch per foot, or 50 at 1/2 inch per foot. Horizontal drainage piping 3 to 6 inches must have at least a 1/8-inch-per-foot slope and uniform alignment and slope. (PC §§ 710.1, 704.1)

If the downstream portion has the same 3-inch fall over 20 feet discussed earlier, its slope is 3/20 = 0.15 inch per foot: it meets the 1/8-inch minimum, but the supplied table gives no capacity at that exact slope, so I can’t determine its allowable DFU load from these columns. Future fixtures provided for must also be counted when sizing the drain. (PC § 710.2)

How many DFU connect to the 3-inch portion, and what is its slope? Those determine whether the supplied building-drain table supports that diameter.

answers.question: Is the primary condensate drain steep enough for the saved cooling-unit example, or does its fall need to change?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:32

The saved example’s fall needs to increase: the minimum is 1/8 inch per horizontal foot, so an 8-foot run requires at least 1 inch of fall; the proposed 1/2 inch is short by 1/2 inch (PC § 314.2.1; MC § 307.2.1). Because overflow could damage the ceiling below and there is no suitably sized and located floor drain, the example also requires one of the listed auxiliary-protection methods; that does not reduce the primary-drain slope requirement (PC § 314.2.3; MC § 307.2.3).

answers.question: Since a blocked drain could damage the ceiling and there is no floor drain, what overflow protection can we use? Do we have to add a separate overflow pipe?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:33

No—you do not have to add a separate overflow pipe. Because a blocked primary condensate drain could damage the ceiling and there is no suitably sized, located floor drain, provide one of the code’s auxiliary-protection methods for the cooling coil (PC § 314.2.3): a separate-drained auxiliary pan; an overflow line connected to the equipment pan; an auxiliary pan with a listed shutoff water-level detector; or a listed detector that shuts off the equipment when the primary drain blocks. The separate overflow line is one option, not the only one. The floor-drain exception does not apply on the facts given.

answers.question: Correction: the primary drain has one inch of total fall over the same eight-foot run. Is the slope now enough, and do we still need the overflow protection?
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:29

Yes. One inch of fall over 8 feet meets the required minimum: 96 inches × 1/8 inch per 12 inches = 1 inch (PC § 314.2.1). Yes, overflow protection is still required in the hypothetical because a blockage could damage the ceiling and no suitably sized and located floor drain is provided. The slope does not replace that separate protection requirement; a separate overflow pipe is only one of the permitted methods (PC § 314.2.3).

answers.question: For a fictional new gas-piping installation in an open outdoor yard in NYC, is 18 inches of earth cover above the top of the pipe enough? There are no protective steel plates, and the run is not underneath a building.
answers.visibleAnswer:
Research complete
00:30

No. For underground gas piping, the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code requires at least 24 inches of cover, measured from grade to the top of the pipe. Eighteen inches is 6 inches short. The less-than-24-inch exception requires the specified steel protective plates, which are absent here (FGC § 404.12). The separate prohibition on piping underground beneath buildings does not apply to the run as described, because it is not beneath a building (FGC § 404.14).
